idiom_name: @State/@Observable owner view passing values and @Binding to child views
implementation_notes: SwiftUI's documented rule is to store data as state in the least common ancestor of the views that need it, making that view the single source of truth, and to pass the data down as read-only properties or as a binding that gives a child two-way access without owning storage. Views are value types, so a child that receives a `let` cannot mutate it: the type system enforces the stateless side of the pattern, and the owner view (or an @Observable model it owns) is the container. State variables mirror the view's life cycle, so they are for transient UI state, not persistence.
pitfalls: SwiftUI views are transient values and must not be shared between view controllers or cached in the container; recreate them and let state, not the view, persist.
@State is view-local storage that disappears with the view: data that must survive navigation or relaunch belongs in an observable model or persistent store, not in the container's own state.
A binding derived from a subscription or computed property can create a write-back cycle when both ends mutate in response to each other.

variants.name: UIKit view controller as stateful container
variants.idiom_name: UIViewController owning the view hierarchy; passive UIView children
variants.implementation_notes: In UIKit the view controller is explicitly the object that updates view contents in response to data changes, responds to user interaction and coordinates with other objects, and it is the sole owner of its view hierarchy - child views are passive displays the controller configures. Container view controllers extend the same role to nested screens through addChild/removeFromParent, so the pattern appears on two levels. Prefer this variant in existing UIKit applications or where imperative control over the view hierarchy is required.
pitfalls: A view controller is the sole owner of its views: never share view instances between controllers (a storyboard gives each controller its own copy, but programmatically created views are yours to keep unique).
Callbacks that capture the controller strongly (or data layers holding the controller) create retain cycles; capture self weakly where the owner already owns the closure.
Updating views from a background thread corrupts layout; marshal state changes onto the main actor or main queue.
